tagline: Mountain passes connect turnpike history, a cog railway and a vanished stone face
intro: The White Mountain Trail makes a 100-mile driving loop through mountain passes and sections of the White Mountain National Forest. White Mountains Attractions Association presents this National Scenic Byway as a route joining mountain scenery, historic landmarks and recreation. In Franconia Notch, the parkway narrows to one lane in each direction between Cannon Mountain and Mount Lafayette.

The crossings had practical work to do before they became a scenic circuit. In 1803, the Tenth New Hampshire Turnpike was extended through Crawford Notch to Lancaster. The turnpike and the later Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad gave settlers northwest of the mountains a route through Conway toward coastal trading ports. The Crawford family built trails and kept inns in the notch during the nineteenth century. The loop’s Kancamagus connection came much later: two dead-end roads were joined in August 1959. Paving followed in 1964, and the first winter plowing came in 1966–67.

From North Woodstock, follow US 3 north through Franconia Notch to Twin Mountain, then US 302 east through Bretton Woods and Crawford Notch to Bartlett. Continue through Glen and south through North Conway to Conway, where the Kancamagus Highway returns west toward Lincoln. That last stretch climbs to 2,855-foot Kancamagus Pass before descending toward Lincoln.

moments.title: Old Man of the Mountain
moments.text: The face depended on the viewpoint: five granite ledges on Cannon Mountain resembled a human profile when seen from the north. The formation stood 1,200 feet above Profile Lake. As freezing and thawing opened cracks, preservation crews added chains, then cement, steel rods and a gutter to divert runoff. It nevertheless collapsed on May 3, 2003. A memorial beside Profile Lake uses steel profilers that align with the cliff to recreate the outline. The rock face is gone, but its image remains on New Hampshire license plates. Its first written mention dates to 1805; it became New Hampshire’s emblem in 1945.

moments.title: Mount Washington Cog Railway
moments.text: Sylvester Marsh’s railway climbs by engaging a toothed wheel with a ladder-like rack with open rungs. It was the world’s first mountain-climbing cog railway. Marsh obtained his charter in 1858, but the Civil War delayed work until 1866. Paying passengers rode the unfinished line in August 1868; construction reached the summit in July 1869. The base road leaves US 302 at Bretton Woods. On the railway, a locomotive pushes a single passenger car uphill and reverses for the descent. Later locomotive designs used slanted boilers so they would stay close to horizontal on the steep track.

moments.title: Crawford Notch
moments.text: US 302 follows the Saco River through the steep-sided pass at Crawford Notch. In August 1826, Samuel Willey’s family and two hired men died in a landslide here. They had left their house for a shelter; the slide destroyed the shelter while leaving the house untouched. An uphill rock outcrop split the slide, which passed on either side of the house and reunited below it. The house later became part of a larger inn and burned in 1898. Mount Willey, on the notch’s western side, bears the family’s name. At the notch’s upper end, Saco Lake supplies the river that runs south through the pass.
